text: LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS: WHAT THEY ARE A large language model (LLM) is a neural network, almost always a transformer, trained on large amounts of text to model the probability of the next token given the previous tokens. LLMs generate text autoregressively, one token at a time, with each new token conditioned on all previous tokens in the context. An LLM does not look up answers in a database of facts when it generates text. Its knowledge is encoded in its weights from training, plus whatever is provided in the prompt or retrieved by tools. Tokens are the units an LLM processes. They are usually subword pieces produced by a tokenizer using algorithms such as byte-pair encoding (BPE), WordPiece, or SentencePiece. A token is not the same as a word. One word can be split into several tokens, and tokenization affects tasks such as counting letters or doing arithmetic. The context window is the maximum number of tokens, including both input and output, that the model can process at once. Text outside the context window is not visible to the model. Instruction tuning, or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), trains the model on prompt-response examples so it follows instructions. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) trains a reward model on human preference comparisons and then optimizes the language model against that reward, often with PPO. Constitutional AI, introduced by Anthropic, uses a set of written principles and AI feedback (RLAIF) to guide model behavior. A model's knowledge cutoff is the point after which events are not represented in its training data. A model does not automatically know about events after its cutoff unless that information is provided at inference time, for example through retrieval or tools. LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS: HALLUCINATIONS AND LIMITATIONS A hallucination is output that is fluent and confident but factually incorrect, unsupported by the source, or fabricated, such as invented citations, quotes, or API functions. Hallucinations occur because LLMs are trained to produce plausible continuations, not to verify truth, and because training rewards guessing over expressing uncertainty. Hallucinations are often divided into intrinsic hallucinations, which contradict the provided source, and extrinsic hallucinations, which cannot be verified from the source. Mitigations include retrieval-augmented generation that grounds answers in retrieved documents, requiring citations, letting models abstain or say they do not know, tool use for calculations and lookups, self-consistency checks, and fact-checking pipelines that extract claims and verify each one against trusted evidence. CLOUD COMPUTING: DEFINITIONS AND SERVICE MODELS NIST Special Publication 800-145 defines cloud computing by five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service. It defines three service models and four deployment models. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) provides virtual machines, storage, and networking, and the customer manages the operating system and everything above it. Amazon EC2 and Google Compute Engine are examples. Platform as a Service (PaaS) provides a managed platform for running applications, so the customer manages the application and its data. Heroku and Google App Engine are examples. Software as a Service (SaaS) delivers complete applications over the internet, such as Gmail or Salesforce. The four deployment models are public cloud, private cloud, community cloud, and hybrid cloud. The shared responsibility model divides security duties between the cloud provider and the customer. The provider secures the underlying infrastructure ("security of the cloud"). The customer secures what they deploy and configure, such as data, identity and access settings, and network rules ("security in the cloud"). On Linux, containers are built on namespaces for isolation and control groups (cgroups) for resource limits. A virtual machine runs a full guest operating system with its own kernel on a hypervisor. AI SAFETY: SCOPE AI safety covers the technical and organizational work of making AI systems behave as intended and avoid causing harm. It includes robustness, alignment, interpretability, evaluation, security, and governance. AI alignment is the problem of making a system's goals and behavior match the intentions and values of its designers and users. AI ethics overlaps with AI safety and focuses on fairness, accountability, transparency, and societal impact. AI SAFETY: ALIGNMENT PROBLEMS Specification gaming, also called reward hacking, occurs when a system optimizes the literal objective it was given in an unintended way that satisfies the metric but not the designer's intent. Goodhart's law, often paraphrased as "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure," describes this dynamic. Outer alignment concerns whether the specified objective captures what we actually want. Inner alignment concerns whether the learned model actually pursues that objective rather than some other goal that happened to work during training. Goal misgeneralization occurs when a model keeps its capabilities in a new situation but pursues an unintended goal. Sycophancy is a tendency of language models to agree with the user or tell users what they want to hear, even when it is incorrect.

AI SAFETY: SECURITY OF AI SYSTEMS Prompt injection is an attack in which input text manipulates a language model into ignoring its instructions or taking unintended actions. Direct prompt injection comes from the user's own input. Indirect prompt injection is hidden in external content the model processes, such as web pages, emails, or retrieved documents. Jailbreaking uses crafted prompts to bypass a model's safety guidelines. Prompt injection has no complete solution. RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION: DEFINITION Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines a retrieval step with a generative language model. Relevant documents are retrieved from an external knowledge source and inserted into the model's context so the model can ground its answer in them. The term was introduced in the 2020 paper "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" by Lewis et al. at Facebook AI Research. RAG lets a system use up-to-date or private information without retraining the model, and it makes it possible to cite sources. RAG: PIPELINE A typical RAG pipeline has an indexing phase and a query phase. In the indexing phase, documents are loaded, split into chunks, converted into embeddings, and stored in a vector index along with metadata. In the query phase, the user's query is embedded, the most similar chunks are retrieved, optionally reranked, and inserted into a prompt. The language model then generates an answer conditioned on that context. RAG: CHUNKING Chunking splits documents into smaller passages before embedding. Common strategies include fixed-size chunks with overlap, splitting on sentences or paragraphs, recursive splitting on document structure, and semantic chunking. Chunks that are too large dilute the embedding with unrelated content and use more of the context window. Chunks that are too small lose context. Chunk size is commonly measured in tokens or words. RAG: RETRIEVAL METHODS Dense retrieval uses embeddings and similarity search. Sparse or lexical retrieval uses term-matching methods such as TF-IDF and BM25. BM25 is a ranking function based on term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization. Lexical retrieval is strong for exact terms, names, codes, and rare words. Dense retrieval is strong for paraphrases and semantic matches. Hybrid search combines both, for example with reciprocal rank fusion. Metadata filtering restricts retrieval by attributes such as source, date, or access permissions. RAG: EVALUATION RAG systems are evaluated on retrieval quality and generation quality separately. Retrieval metrics include recall@k, precision@k, mean reciprocal rank (MRR), and normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG). Generation is assessed for faithfulness (also called groundedness), meaning whether the answer is supported by the retrieved context, and for answer relevance, meaning whether it addresses the question. Faithfulness to the retrieved context is different from factual correctness, because the retrieved context itself can be wrong or outdated. Frameworks such as RAGAS provide automated RAG evaluation metrics, often using an LLM as a judge. RAG: FAILURE MODES AND MISCONCEPTIONS RAG reduces hallucinations but does not eliminate them. Failure modes include retrieving irrelevant or incomplete chunks, missing relevant documents, the model ignoring or contradicting the retrieved context, the model adding unsupported details beyond the context, and conflicts between the model's training knowledge and the retrieved text. SOFTWARE ENGINEERING: DESIGN PRINCIPLES SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles popularized by Robert C. Martin. S is the Single Responsibility Principle: a class should have one reason to change. O is the Open/Closed Principle: software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. L is the Liskov Substitution Principle, from Barbara Liskov: objects of a subtype should be usable anywhere the base type is expected without breaking correctness. I is the Interface Segregation Principle: clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. D is the Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level modules. DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) comes from the book The Pragmatic Programmer. ALGORITHMS: ASYMPTOTIC ANALYSIS Big O notation gives an asymptotic upper bound on the growth of a function. Big Omega gives an asymptotic lower bound, and Big Theta gives a tight bound, meaning both an upper and a lower bound. A common misconception is that Big O means "worst case." Big O is a bound on a function, and it can describe the worst case, the average case, or the best case of an algorithm. Worst-case, average-case, and best-case analysis are separate questions from which asymptotic notation is used. Constant factors and lower-order terms are dropped in asymptotic notation, so 3n^2 + 5n + 7 is Theta(n^2). An algorithm with a better asymptotic bound is not always faster in practice for small inputs, because constant factors, memory access patterns, and cache behavior matter. Amortized analysis gives the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations. Amortized cost is not the same as average-case cost over random inputs. The common growth classes in increasing order are constant O(1), logarithmic O(log n), linear O(n), linearithmic O(n log n), quadratic O(n^2), cubic O(n^3), exponential O(2^n), and factorial O(n!). In asymptotic notation the base of a logarithm does not matter, because logarithms with

It halves the search range on each step and runs in O(log n) time. Binary search on a linked list is not efficient, because reaching the middle element takes linear time. A classic bug in binary search is integer overflow when the midpoint is computed as (low + high) / 2 in fixed-width integer languages. Computing low + (high - low) / 2 avoids it. TRANSFORMERS: ORIGIN AND STRUCTURE The transformer architecture was introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need" by Vaswani et al. at Google. It was originally designed for machine translation and used an encoder-decoder structure. Transformers do not use recurrence or convolution. They rely on attention mechanisms, which lets them process all positions of a sequence in parallel during training, unlike recurrent neural networks. A common misconception is that transformers rely on recurrent layers to handle long-range dependencies. Transformers replaced recurrence with self-attention. In the original transformer, each encoder layer has a multi-head self-attention sublayer followed by a position-wise feed-forward network. Each sublayer is wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization. Each decoder layer adds a cross-attention sublayer that attends to the encoder's output. The original base model had 6 encoder layers, 6 decoder layers, a model dimension of 512, and 8 attention heads. Without non-linear activation functions, a stack of linear layers is equivalent to a single linear transformation. The universal approximation theorem states that a feedforward network with a single hidden layer and enough units can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain to arbitrary accuracy. The theorem says nothing about how to find those weights or how many units are needed. Common activation functions include ReLU (rectified linear unit), which is max(0, x); sigmoid, which maps to (0, 1); tanh, which maps to (-1, 1); and GELU and SiLU/Swish, which are smooth variants used in many transformers. Softmax converts a vector of scores into a probability distribution that sums to 1 and is typically used in the output layer for multi-class classification. A dynamic array, such as a Python list, a Java ArrayList, or a C++ std::vector, grows by allocating a larger block, typically a constant-factor larger, and copying the elements. This gives amortized O(1) appends even though an individual append can take O(n) time. A linked list stores nodes that point to the next node, and in a doubly linked list also to the previous node. Access by position takes O(n) time. Insertion or deletion takes O(1) time once you already hold a reference to the right node. A common misconception is that linked lists are always faster than arrays for insertion. Finding the insertion point still takes O(n) time, and linked lists have poor cache locality. A foreign key references a primary or unique key in another table and enforces referential integrity. SQL is a declarative language: a query describes what result is wanted, and the database's query planner decides how to compute it. SQL is standardized by ISO/IEC 9075, but database systems implement different subsets and add their own extensions. In SQL, NULL represents a missing or unknown value. Most aggregate functions, such as SUM and AVG, ignore NULL values. COUNT(*) counts all rows, while COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not NULL.
